*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week2-2026-10-12)*

## What I Built

**One product photo. About a minute. A full marketing kit.**

That's Mochi. You give it a photo and a few true facts. It gives you studio photos, an image deck, a 10-second vertical video, and copy for each platform you sell on. Every piece is built on your own computer, with open models.

Here is why I built it.

### I used to run an ecommerce brand

In small ecommerce, performance marketing is everything. If your ad is not live, you are not selling.

And making one ad was a slog. For every single product I had to:

- Get listing copy from two or three different AI chats, then stitch it together by hand
- Write the ad copy
- Edit the photos
- Generate the images for the listing
- Make video ads

Every step lived in a different tool. Every handoff was a copy and paste.

It cost me in three ways:

- **Time.** The slow part was never the idea. It was the gap between "I have a product" and "it's live". Every day in that gap was a lost sale.
- **Cashflow.** A subscription for images, one for video, one for copy, one for editing. In a small business, cashflow is tight, and tool bills quietly eat it.
- **Privacy.** My product details, my pricing and my workflow all sat inside other people's tools. None of it was ever private.

### Then I watched my mom do the same thing

My mom is a cosmetician. She sells skincare and beauty products.

To post one Instagram reel or one Facebook post, she goes through **3 to 4 different apps**:

1. Canva for the image
2. CapCut, or another editor, for the video
3. ChatGPT or Claude for the caption, then back and forth, copy, paste, "make it shorter", copy, paste again
4. Then the post itself, on each platform

**One single image post took her 3 to 4 hours.**

Those are hours she could have spent with customers. Instead she was learning video editors and rewriting captions. She is good at selling. The tools were making her a part-time designer.

That is the problem. It isn't "AI can't make content". It's that the work is split across too many tools, costs too much attention, and sends your product details to places you don't control.

### The fix: one flow, on your own machine

Mochi turns that whole chain into three taps.

<!-- DEV ignores relative paths, so use the raw GitHub URL once the images are pushed -->
![Mochi landing page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/landing-hero-desktop.png)

You get:

- **Studio photos.** Your phone photo, cut out and placed on a designed backdrop, with the product itself never repainted
- **An image deck.** Slides ready for a feed or a catalog
- **A 10-second vertical video.** Camera moves and text cards built from your own copy
- **Platform copy.** Listing, social, Pinterest and a video brief, written for each place you sell

One thing I care about more than anything: **Mochi does not make things up.** If you didn't tell it your product is waterproof, the copy won't say so. Missing facts are listed back to you ("Not provided, so left out of the copy"). Risky claims get flagged before you post.

For a skincare seller, that matters. "Reduces wrinkles" is a legal claim, not a style choice.

### How to use it

It is three steps, and the draft saves itself as you go.

1. **Photos.** Add up to 5 photos. The first one is the main one.
2. **Facts.** Mochi reads your photos and pre-fills the form: product name, a short summary, and any text it can read on the label. Each of those is tagged **"From photo, check it"**, so you stay in charge. Blank fields are flagged as missing. They are never guessed.
3. **Style.** Pick where you sell (Instagram, Facebook, Pinterest, Etsy, Shopify), a tone, a goal, a backdrop, and a writing speed.

Then tap **Generate kit**. You can leave the page while it works. When it's done you get four tabs: **Overview, Copy, Photos, Share**.

Nothing posts on its own. The only thing Mochi can send anywhere is a Shopify **draft**, and only when you tap it.

## Demo

**Video:** **[TODO: paste the YouTube link here as `{% embed https://youtu.be/YOUR_ID %}`]**

**Try the demo studio:** [mochi-demo.onrender.com](https://mochi-demo.onrender.com)

I'll be honest about what that link is. It's the landing page plus a studio that runs entirely **in your browser**. It's labelled as a demo. It does **not** run the real models, because they need a computer with a GPU, and I won't pretend otherwise. The full app is the code below, running on your own machine. The first user session further down is the real thing.

## Code

{% embed https://github.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft %}

Backend: FastAPI, SQLite, Pydantic. Frontend: Next.js 16 and React 19. 135 backend tests pass. Every number in this post can be reproduced from the files in `backend/finetune/results/`, with the commands in [`docs/RESULTS.md`](https://github.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/blob/main/docs/RESULTS.md).

## How I Built It

### The big picture

A request makes two lanes run **at the same time**: one for visuals and one for language. They meet at the deck and the video, which need the finished copy.

![System architecture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/system.png)

The page polls the job every 1.5 seconds and shows real progress and partial copy as it arrives. Nothing is faked.

### Which model does which job

Every model has **one job and one strict contract**.

| Model or tool | Job |
|---|---|
| **Gemma 3 4B** (Ollama) | Fast copy (the default), reading photos |
| **Gemma 3 12B** (Ollama) | Best-quality copy, and the independent judge in my evaluation |
| **rembg** (U2-Net) | Cuts the product out of its background |
| **OpenCV, NumPy, Pillow** | Measure, denoise, 2x upscale, fix tone, build the deck. Deterministic. |
| **FFmpeg** | The video. Camera moves, crossfades, text cards. **Not** generative video. |
| **Qwen3.5-4B + LoRA** (Tinker) | My fine-tuned copy writer |
| **A plain-code checker** | Scores and flags the copy |

Two choices worth explaining.

**The video is not AI-generated.** It's image processing plus FFmpeg. That means the product in the video is *your* product, pixel for pixel. Generative video tends to repaint the product, and a seller can't sell a product that looks different from the real one.

**The checker is plain code, not a second model.** A model can talk itself into anything. A word list and a number check can't.

### Photos to studio shots

![Studio imagery pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/studio.png)

Measure the photo, cut out the product, clean the product's pixels, fix the tone, choose a backdrop that suits what the photo shows, then compose. If the cutout looks wrong (too little or too much of the frame), it falls back to a framed photo instead of a bad cutout.

### The copy pipeline

![Copy pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/copy.png)

The kit is split into small parts that run in parallel: four core parts plus one per platform. Each part's output is forced into a JSON schema. A bad call is retried once, and only the missing parts are redone. Then plain code checks for forbidden words, invented numbers and unsupported claims, and anything it finds is shown to the seller.

### Why it's fast

![Where the time goes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/optimisations.png)

My first version was far too slow. One big generation on a laptop took 90 to 145 seconds. Three changes fixed most of it:

| Change | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Fast mode (Gemma 4B) as the default | copy 53 s | copy 14 s |
| Split the kit into parallel parts | one 12B call, 90 to 145 s | 45 to 60 s |
| Run the visual and language lanes together | the sum of both | the slower lane, plus a few seconds |

A four-photo kit went from about **100 s to about 18 s** in Fast mode. Best quality (Gemma 12B) takes about 57 s.

The trade-off is real. The 4B model gets more claims flagged than the 12B. The post-check still catches them, and Best quality is one switch away.

### Training a small model to follow the rules

This is the part I'm proudest of, and the part where I got it wrong first.

![Fine-tuning pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/finetune.png)

The idea: a big teacher model writes marketing kits, code and an independent judge reject any kit that breaks the rules, and only the **clean** kits are used to train a small student. The full story and numbers are in the Tinker section below.

### Privacy by design

![What stays local and what can leave](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/trust.png)

Your product facts stay on your computer. The only things that can ever leave are a Shopify draft you tap, and scrubbed Sentry metadata. Both are covered in the sections below.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Go back to my two stories. In both, the real cost was not money alone. It was **control**.

**1. Your product details are your business.**
Pricing, ingredients, launch plans, the way you describe your product. With open models running locally, all of it stays on your machine. There is no "we don't train on your data" to trust. The data never leaves.

**2. A fixed price of zero, per kit.**
On your own computer, every kit costs electricity. A seller can run it five times on one product, try three tones, and never wonder if it is "worth" the credits. In a business where cashflow is tight, that matters.

**3. I could change the model, not just the prompt.**
The most important thing I did in this project was fine-tune a small open model so it follows one rule better: *don't invent claims*. Prompting alone left the 4B model at 23% clean kits. Training took it to 88%. You can't do that to a closed model, and you can't download what you trained.

**4. I could look inside and measure.**
I saw that my first fine-tune had learned to pass my word list while still embellishing. I only found that out because I could test it against a second model. With a closed API I'd have had one number and no way to question it.

**5. One setting swaps the model.**
Fast or Best quality is a single setting, and both are open Gemma models. The next Gemma release is a one-line change.

The honest limit: open models on your own computer need a computer that can run them. That is why the public demo is a browser demo, and why I wrote the local setup into the README.

## My Agent Session

I built Mochi with Claude Code, and every session is recorded with **Entire**. Each commit carries the checkpoint of the conversation that produced it.

- [`docs/DECISIONS.md`](https://github.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/blob/main/docs/DECISIONS.md) lists **19 decisions**, each with its reason, its commit and its Entire checkpoint ID
- About **113 checkpoints** are pushed to the repo
- To read one: `entire checkpoint explain <id>` in a clone of the repo

A few of the decisions the record shows, in my own words:

- **#8: re-scoring my own fine-tune.** I tightened the checker and my "93% clean" model became 65%. I recorded that instead of hiding it.
- **#13: cutting ElevenLabs.** I planned an AI voiceover, then dropped it so the time went to the fine-tune, tracing and a real user.
- **#16: making Fast the default.** Stage timings showed copy was the slowest part, so the default became the smaller model.

One caveat on honesty: checkpoints for work from before Entire was switched on were *imported* from my local history and matched to commits by time. Read those as "the conversation this came out of", not a one-to-one record. The decisions file says the same.

## Prize Categories

I'm entering **Tinker, Gemma, Sentry Agent Tracing and Entire**, and I'm mentioning Render for the demo. Each section covers what I used, why, what it was meant to fix, and what I found.

### Best Use of Tinker

**What I used it for.** I fine-tuned **Qwen3.5-4B with a LoRA adapter** on Tinker to write marketing copy that follows one rule: *never invent a claim the seller didn't give.*

**Why Tinker.** Prompting a small model to follow that rule didn't work. Untuned Qwen3.5-4B produced a clean kit only 18% of the time. I wanted to change the model, not keep rewording the prompt, and Tinker let me train without running my own GPU servers.

**How it worked.**

1. A big teacher model, **Qwen3.5-397B-A17B**, writes and revises kits on Tinker
2. My checker and an independent judge reject any kit with an invented claim, number or forbidden word
3. The teacher revises with the checker's findings, at most 2 rounds
4. Only kits with **zero** hard violations become training data
5. A small student is trained on those: rank 32, 3 epochs, 319 examples, learning rate 2e-4
6. A held-out set of 60 products, which the training code refuses to read, tests it

The whole thing cost **$5.41 of the $10 credit**.

**Results** (60 held-out synthetic products, one checker):

![Evaluation results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/evaluation.png)

| Model | Clean kits | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.5-4B, untuned | 18% | 10 to 28% |
| Gemma 3 4B | 23% | 13 to 35% |
| Gemma 3 12B | 45% | 33 to 57% |
| Fine-tune v1 | 65% | 53 to 77% |
| **Fine-tune v2** | **88%** | **78 to 95%** |

That's a model of a fraction of Gemma 12B's size, producing nearly twice as many clean kits, and about 10 times faster (4.9 s against 48.7 s per kit, though v2 runs on Tinker's cloud and Gemma on my laptop).

**What I got wrong first, and what it taught me.** v1 scored **93%** clean under my first checker. Then I tightened it to catch number words, urgency and occasions, and the same outputs scored **65%**. v1 had learned to pass my word list.

So I added a second opinion: an independent judge from a different model family (Gemma 12B) that lists every statement the facts don't support. On that judge, **v1 was worse than the untuned model** (0.63 flags per kit against 0.43). Same trap, confirmed by a second measure.

v2 fixes that by training only on kits that passed **both** the checker and the judge.

**The honest result on the judge.** v2 halves the untuned model's flags (0.43 to 0.20), but the confidence intervals overlap, and Gemma 12B is lower still at 0.13. With 30 kits per model I can't claim more than that.

**Limits I'm stating on purpose:**
- The test set is synthetic, and the checker also filtered the training data
- The fine-tune runs on Tinker, so its inputs leave the machine. The app's default (Gemma via Ollama) stays local.
- The fine-tune is **not** in the app's path yet. I haven't exported it to GGUF for Ollama.
- Hosted cost is about $3 per 1,000 kits, estimated from token counts

**What I learned.** A fine-tune can look great while learning the wrong lesson. The only reason I caught it is that I measured it twice, with two different judges, and wrote both down.

### Best Use of Gemma

**What I used it for.** Gemma does three jobs inside Mochi, all through Ollama on the seller's own computer:

1. **The copy writer.** Gemma 3 4B for Fast, Gemma 3 12B for Best quality
2. **The photo reader.** It reads up to 5 photos and returns suggested facts, each tagged "From photo, check it"
3. **The independent judge.** Gemma 3 12B, a different family from the Qwen teacher, reviews kits in my evaluation

**Why Gemma.** It's open-weight, it runs on one machine, and it can be held to a JSON schema. That matters here: the seller's facts shouldn't leave their computer, and every part of a kit must come back as strict, checkable JSON.

**What it was meant to fix.** The cost and privacy problems from my ecommerce days: no per-kit fee, and nothing sent to anyone else's server.

**Results.**

- Both sizes run the same prompt and the same checker, so I could compare them fairly: **23% clean kits on 4B and 45% on 12B**
- Speed is the trade-off. Fast (4B) builds a four-photo kit in about **18 s**, Best quality (12B) in about **57 s**
- As the judge, Gemma 12B had the fewest flags of any model I tested (0.13 per kit)

**What I learned.** Two things. First, the model size is a user choice, not a technical one, so I made it a switch on the form. Second, the judge is Gemma, so it may be lenient toward Gemma's own writing. That bias favours the Gemma rows and works *against* my fine-tune's claim, so it can't be inflating my result.

### Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing

**What I used it for.** Tracing every model call and every job, without Sentry ever seeing a seller's product facts.

**Why this was the hard part.** A marketing tool handles a seller's most private material: product details, prices, plans. Sending prompts to a tracing service would break the promise the whole product makes. So the question was not "can I trace this", it was "can I trace this and prove nothing private leaks".

**What Sentry sees.**

![What Sentry sees, and what it never sees](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/observability.png)

- Each model call is a **`gen_ai.chat` span**, with the model, token counts and latency
- Each generation job is a transaction
- Each flagged claim is an issue (which rule fired, and how many)
- Each seller report is an event. The report button sends a section name and a fixed reason code, **never free text**

**What it never sees.** An allow-list scrubber removes everything that is not on the list of allowed metadata. Product facts, copy, photos and prompts can't pass it.

**How I know it works.** A canary test pushes a unique fake product through every input path of the real app, then fails if that marker shows up in *any* outgoing Sentry payload. It's in `tests/test_tracing.py`.

**Results and honesty.** The scrubber and the canary test are in place and pass. I am **not** claiming Sentry has caught a real production incident, because it hasn't. Mochi has had one real user session, not production traffic.

**What I learned.** Making tracing safe was a bigger design question than turning it on. The allow-list approach (what's permitted, not what's blocked) is the one that survives new fields being added later.

### Best Use of Entire

**What I used it for.** To record how Mochi was built, so a reader can see *why* the code is the way it is, not just what it does.

**Why.** Most repos show a result. For a project where I changed my mind several times, the changes are the story. A re-scored fine-tune, a cut feature and a new default each have a reason that a commit message can't hold.

**What came of it.**

- **About 113 checkpoints** of Claude Code sessions, pushed to the repo
- [`docs/DECISIONS.md`](https://github.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/blob/main/docs/DECISIONS.md): **19 numbered decisions**, each with the reason, the commit and the Entire checkpoint ID
- Anyone can run `entire checkpoint explain <id>` in a clone and read the prompts, files and reasoning behind a decision

**The most useful example.** Decision #8 records the day my fine-tune went from 93% to 65% under a stricter checker. That is the kind of moment that normally disappears. Here it is written down, with the conversation that led to it.

**Honest limit.** Checkpoints from before Entire was enabled were imported from local history and matched by time. They show the conversation a commit came out of, not a one-to-one record.

### Render (mentioned, with limits)

The public demo at [mochi-demo.onrender.com](https://mochi-demo.onrender.com) is deployed on Render from a `render.yaml` Blueprint, on the free plan.

That's a static front end plus an in-browser demo, with **no model running on Render**. I'm not claiming Render as an AI runtime. It's there so anyone can try the interface without installing anything. The real product runs on your own machine.

---

**What's next:** exporting the fine-tune to GGUF so it can run in Ollama with everything else, a real-seller evaluation instead of a synthetic one, and more first-user sessions.

If you sell something and make your own content, I'd love to hear what's missing. Tell me in the comments.

*Built solo, with Claude Code.*

26	In small ecommerce, performance marketing is everything. If your ad is not live, you are not selling.
27	
28	And making one ad was a slog. For every single product I had to:
29	
30	- Get listing copy from two or three different AI chats, then stitch it together by hand
31	- Write the ad copy
32	- Edit the photos
33	- Generate the images for the listing
34	- Make video ads
35	
36	Every step lived in a different tool. Every handoff was a copy and paste.
37	
38	It cost me in three ways:
39	
40	- **Time.** The slow part was never the idea. It was the gap between "I have a product" and "it's live". Every day in that gap was a lost sale.
41	- **Cashflow.** A subscription for images, one for video, one for copy, one for editing. In a small business, cashflow is tight, and tool bills quietly eat it.
42	- **Privacy.** My product details, my pricing and my workflow all sat inside other people's tools. None of it was ever private.
43	
44	### Then I watched my mom do the same thing
45	
46	My mom is a cosmetician. She sells skincare and beauty products.
47	
48	To post one Instagram reel or one Facebook post, she goes through **3 to 4 different apps**:
49	
50	1. Canva for the image
51	2. CapCut, or another editor, for the video
52	3. ChatGPT or Claude for the caption, then back and forth, copy, paste, "make it shorter", copy, paste again
53	4. Then the post itself, on each platform
54	
55	**One single image post took her 3 to 4 hours.**
56	
57	Those are hours she could have spent with customers. Instead she was learning video editors and rewriting captions. She is good at selling. The tools were making her a part-time designer.
58	
59	That is the problem. It isn't "AI can't make content". It's that the work is split across too many tools, costs too much attention, and sends your product details to places you don't control.
60	
61	### The fix: one flow, on your own machine
62	
63	Mochi turns that whole chain into three taps.
64	
65	<!-- DEV ignores relative paths, so use the raw GitHub URL once the images are pushed -->
66	![Mochi landing page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/landing-hero-desktop.png)

73	- **Platform copy.** Listing, social, Pinterest and a video brief, written for each place you sell

263	I'm entering **Tinker, Gemma, Sentry Agent Tracing and Entire**, and I'm mentioning Render for the demo. Each section covers what I used, why, what it was meant to fix, and what I found.
264	
265	### Best Use of Tinker
266	
267	**What I used it for.** I fine-tuned **Qwen3.5-4B with a LoRA adapter** on Tinker to write marketing copy that follows one rule: *never invent a claim the seller didn't give.*
268	
269	**Why Tinker.** Prompting a small model to follow that rule didn't work. Untuned Qwen3.5-4B produced a clean kit only 18% of the time. I wanted to change the model, not keep rewording the prompt, and Tinker let me train without running my own GPU servers.
270	
271	**How it worked.**
272	
273	1. A big teacher model, **Qwen3.5-397B-A17B**, writes and revises kits on Tinker
274	2. My checker and an independent judge reject any kit with an invented claim, number or forbidden word
275	3. The teacher revises with the checker's findings, at most 2 rounds
276	4. Only kits with **zero** hard violations become training data
277	5. A small student is trained on those: rank 32, 3 epochs, 319 examples, learning rate 2e-4
278	6. A held-out set of 60 products, which the training code refuses to read, tests it
279	
280	The whole thing cost **$5.41 of the $10 credit**.
281	
282	**Results** (60 held-out synthetic products, one checker):
283	
284	![Evaluation results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/evaluation.png)
285	
286	| Model | Clean kits | 95% CI |
287	|---|---|---|
288	| Qwen3.5-4B, untuned | 18% | 10 to 28% |
289	| Gemma 3 4B | 23% | 13 to 35% |
290	| Gemma 3 12B | 45% | 33 to 57% |
291	| Fine-tune v1 | 65% | 53 to 77% |
292	| **Fine-tune v2** | **88%** | **78 to 95%** |
293	
294	That's a 4B model, a third of Gemma 12B's size, producing nearly twice as many clean kits, and about 10 times faster (4.9 s against 48.7 s per kit, though v2 runs on Tinker's cloud and Gemma on my laptop).
295	
296	**What I got wrong first, and what it taught me.** v1 scored **93%** clean under my first checker. Then I tightened it to catch number words, urgency and occasions, and the same outputs scored **65%**. v1 had learned to pass my word list.
297	
298	So I added a second opinion: an independent judge from a different model family (Gemma 12B) that lists every statement the facts don't support. On that judge, **v1 was worse than the untuned model** (0.63 flags per kit against 0.43). Same trap, confirmed by a second measure.
299	
300	v2 fixes that by training only on kits that passed **both** the checker and the judge.
301	
302	**The honest result on the judge.** v2 halves the untuned model's flags (0.43 to 0.20), but the confidence intervals overlap, and Gemma 12B is lower still at 0.13. With 30 kits per model I can't claim more than that.
303	
304	**Limits I'm stating on purpose:**
305	- The test set is synthetic, and the checker also filtered the training data
306	- The fine-tune runs on Tinker, so its inputs leave the machine. The app's default (Gemma via Ollama) stays local.
307	- The fine-tune is **not** in the app's path yet. I haven't exported it to GGUF for Ollama.
308	- Hosted cost is about $3 per 1,000 kits, estimated from token counts
309	
310	**What I learned.** A fine-tune can look great while learning the wrong lesson. The only reason I caught it is that I measured it twice, with two different judges, and wrote both down.
311	
312	### Best Use of Gemma
313	
314	**What I used it for.** Gemma does three jobs inside Mochi, all through Ollama on the seller's own computer:
315	
316	1. **The copy writer.** Gemma 3 4B for Fast, Gemma 3 12B for Best quality
317	2. **The photo reader.** It reads up to 5 photos and returns suggested facts, each tagged "From photo, check it"
318	3. **The independent judge.** Gemma 3 12B, a different family from the Qwen teacher, reviews kits in my evaluation
319	
320	**Why Gemma.** It's open-weight, it runs on one machine, and it can be held to a JSON schema. That matters here: the seller's facts shouldn't leave their computer, and every part of a kit must come back as strict, checkable JSON.
321	
322	**What it was meant to fix.** The cost and privacy problems from my ecommerce days: no per-kit fee, and nothing sent to anyone else's server.
323	
324	**Results.**
325	
326	- Both sizes run the same prompt and the same checker, so I could compare them fairly: **23% clean kits on 4B and 45% on 12B**
327	- Speed is the trade-off. Fast (4B) builds a four-photo kit in about **18 s**, Best quality (12B) in about **57 s**
328	- As the judge, Gemma 12B had the fewest flags of any model I tested (0.13 per kit)
329	
330	**What I learned.** Two things. First, the model size is a user choice, not a technical one, so I made it a switch on the form. Second, the judge is Gemma, so it may be lenient toward Gemma's own writing. That bias favours the Gemma rows and works *against* my fine-tune's claim, so it can't be inflating my result.
331	
332	### Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing
333	
334	**What I used it for.** Tracing every model call and every job, without Sentry ever seeing a seller's product facts.
335	
336	**Why this was the hard part.** A marketing tool handles a seller's most private material: product details, prices, plans. Sending prompts to a tracing service would break the promise the whole product makes. So the question was not "can I trace this", it was "can I trace this and prove nothing private leaks".
337	
338	**What Sentry sees.**
339	
340	![What Sentry sees, and what it never sees](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/observability.png)
341	
342	- Each model call is a **`gen_ai.chat` span**, with the model, token counts and latency
343	- Each generation job is a transaction
344	- Each flagged claim is an issue (which rule fired, and how many)
345	- Each seller report is an event. The report button sends a section name and a fixed reason code, **never free text**
346	
347	**What it never sees.** An allow-list scrubber removes everything that is not on the list of allowed metadata. Product facts, copy, photos and prompts can't pass it.
348	
349	**How I know it works.** A canary test pushes a unique fake product through every input path of the real app, then fails if that marker shows up in *any* outgoing Sentry payload. It's in `tests/test_tracing.py`.

349	**How I know it works.** A canary test pushes a unique fake product through every input path of the real app, then fails if that marker shows up in *any* outgoing Sentry payload. It's in `tests/test_tracing.py`.
350	
351	**Results and honesty.** The scrubber and the canary test are in place and pass. I am **not** claiming Sentry has caught a real production incident, because it hasn't. Mochi has had one real user session, not production traffic.
352	
353	**What I learned.** Making tracing safe was a bigger design question than turning it on. The allow-list approach (what's permitted, not what's blocked) is the one that survives new fields being added later.
354	
355	### Best Use of Entire
356	
357	**What I used it for.** To record how Mochi was built, so a reader can see *why* the code is the way it is, not just what it does.
358	
359	**Why.** Most repos show a result. For a project where I changed my mind several times, the changes are the story. A re-scored fine-tune, a cut feature and a new default each have a reason that a commit message can't hold.
360	
361	**What came of it.**
362	
363	- **About 113 checkpoints** of Claude Code sessions, pushed to the repo
364	- [`docs/DECISIONS.md`](https://github.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/blob/main/docs/DECISIONS.md): **19 numbered decisions**, each with the reason, the commit and the Entire checkpoint ID
365	- Anyone can run `entire checkpoint explain <id>` in a clone and read the prompts, files and reasoning behind a decision
366	
367	**The most useful example.** Decision #8 records the day my fine-tune went from 93% to 65% under a stricter checker. That is the kind of moment that normally disappears. Here it is written down, with the conversation that led to it.
368	
369	**Honest limit.** Checkpoints from before Entire was enabled were imported from local history and matched by time. They show the conversation a commit came out of, not a one-to-one record.
370

372	
373	The public demo at [mochi-demo.onrender.com](https://mochi-demo.onrender.com) is deployed on Render from a `render.yaml` Blueprint, on the free plan.
374	
375	That's a static front end plus an in-browser demo, with **no model running on Render**. I'm not claiming Render as an AI runtime. It's there so anyone can try the interface without installing anything. The real product runs on your own machine.
376	
377	---

380

147	## How I Built It
148	
149	### The big picture
150	
151	A request makes two lanes run **at the same time**: one for visuals and one for language. They meet at the deck and the video, which need the finished copy.
152	
153	![System architecture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/system.png)
154	
155	The page polls the job every 1.5 seconds and shows real progress and partial copy as it arrives. Nothing is faked.
156	
157	### Which model does which job
158	
159	Every model has **one job and one strict contract**.
160	
161	| Model or tool | Job |
162	|---|---|
163	| **Gemma 3 4B** (Ollama) | Fast copy (the default), reading photos |
164	| **Gemma 3 12B** (Ollama) | Best-quality copy, and the independent judge in my evaluation |
165	| **rembg** (U2-Net) | Cuts the product out of its background |
166	| **OpenCV, NumPy, Pillow** | Measure, denoise, 2x upscale, fix tone, build the deck. Deterministic. |
167	| **FFmpeg** | The video. Camera moves, crossfades, text cards. **Not** generative video. |
168	| **Qwen3.5-4B + LoRA** (Tinker) | My fine-tuned copy writer |
169	| **A plain-code checker** | Scores and flags the copy |
170	
171	Two choices worth explaining.
172	
173	**The video is not AI-generated.** It's image processing plus FFmpeg. That means the product in the video is *your* product, pixel for pixel. Generative video tends to repaint the product, and a seller can't sell a product that looks different from the real one.
174	
175	**The checker is plain code, not a second model.** A model can talk itself into anything. A word list and a number check can't.
176	
177	### Photos to studio shots
178	
179	![Studio imagery pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/studio.png)
180	
181	Measure the photo, cut out the product, clean the product's pixels, fix the tone, choose a backdrop that suits what the photo shows, then compose. If the cutout looks wrong (too little or too much of the frame), it falls back to a framed photo instead of a bad cutout.
182	
183	### The copy pipeline
184	
185	![Copy pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/copy.png)
186	
187	The kit is split into small parts that run in parallel: four core parts plus one per platform. Each part's output is forced into a JSON schema. A bad call is retried once, and only the missing parts are redone. Then plain code checks for forbidden words, invented numbers and unsupported claims, and anything it finds is shown to the seller.
188	
189	### Why it's fast
190	
191	![Where the time goes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/diagrams/optimisations.png)
192	
193	My first version was far too slow. One big generation on a laptop took 90 to 145 seconds. Three changes fixed most of it:
194	
195	| Change | Before | After |
196	|---|---|---|
197	| Fast mode (Gemma 4B) as the default | copy 53 s | copy 14 s |
198	| Split the kit into parallel parts | one 12B call, 90 to 145 s | 45 to 60 s |
199	| Run the visual and language lanes together | the sum of both | the slower lane, plus a few seconds |
200	
201	A four-photo kit went from about **100 s to about 18 s** in Fast mode. Best quality (Gemma 12B) takes about 57 s.
202	
203	The trade-off is real. The 4B model gets more claims flagged than the 12B. The post-check still catches them, and Best quality is one switch away.
204	
205	### Training a small model to follow the rules
206	
207	This is the part I'm proudest of.
208

Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend Submission 🤝
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend

A practice call in Before I Call: a Japanese question with furigana, a word's meaning on hover, then a plain-English explanation of the question

I've lived alone in Tokyo for four years now, but when my washing machine started leaking, I stared at the building manager's number for twenty minutes before I pressed call.

My friend ran into the same thing when she had to cancel her internet contract by phone. The provider's explanation sounded alien to her. The Japanese businesses use on the phone is not the Japanese you use every day, and on a call there's no face to read and no time to look anything up.

So I built Before I Call, an app where you practice the call with an AI before you make the real one. I made it for myself and for friends in the same situation, and sent it to one of them to see if it actually helps. Their reply is further down.

Here it is in action:



What I Built
You describe the call you need to make, or pick one of the examples (home repairs, the clinic, a missed delivery, the city office, dietary requests, lost property, bills). Then you talk to an AI that plays the person on the other end, like a receptionist or your building manager. It speaks polite Japanese, asks one question at a time and waits for your answer. There's no score.

If you get stuck, you don't have to hang up. Explain question opens a helper next to the call with what the question means and a reply you could give. The AI on the call doesn't see it, so the role-play carries on. Slow replay plays the question again at 0.7x speed, and Repeat question asks the AI to say it again. Kanji have furigana, every line has romaji, and known words show their meaning when you hover or tap.

When you say goodbye, the AI hangs up and you get a call card: the whole conversation with readings and meanings, and a list of useful words from your call. You can download it as a PDF and keep it next to you when you make the real call.

It won't make up dates, prices or availability, and it can't book anything for you. It's only for practice.

Setting up a call. You can type or dictate it in English or Japanese, or start from an example. Enhance prompt tidies up rough notes without adding facts you didn't give it.

The setup form: a washing-machine leak typed in English, with Start from an example, Enhance prompt, Dictate situation and Start voice practice

Asking for help in the middle of the call:

The explanation dialog: the question's meaning, a note on どうされましたか, and a suggested reply with furigana

The word list on the call card:

The call card's useful words: 管理会社, 田中 and 洗濯機 with furigana, romaji and English meanings

What my friend said
I sent the link to my friend on WhatsApp and asked them to let me know if it helps. This is what came back:

WhatsApp chat: I share the Before I Call link with my friend. They reply 

I didn't expect the PDF to be the part they liked. I made it as a cheat sheet for the real call, but for someone studying for the JLPT it's also a word list from a conversation they actually had.

Demo
Try it at before-i-call.onrender.com. There's no sign-up. Voice practice needs a microphone. Without one, tap Play guided example to watch a recorded call in Japanese or English.

The PDF call card: the situation, each turn as a speech bubble with furigana, romaji and meaning

 Before I Call home page: practice a phone call in Japanese or English, or play a guided example
The problem
A phone call is the hardest everyday conversation in a second language. There is no face to read and no time to look anything up, and the other person speaks at native speed. People who live in Japan put off calling the building manager, the clinic or the delivery company, not because they can't manage the conversation, but because the call itself feels risky.

Phrasebooks help with the first sentence. They don't…
View on GitHub
MIT licensed and built during the challenge. It has 87 tests (80 Python, 7 Node), and the README explains how to run it locally.

How I Built It
The call runs on ElevenLabs Agents
The live call is an ElevenLabs agent. It handles all the audio: the WebRTC connection, speech recognition, working out when you've finished speaking, interruptions, and the voice. I use one agent for every scenario. When a call starts, the app sends that call's prompt, first line, language and voice as overrides, so the same agent can be a Japanese building manager or an English clinic receptionist.

I slowed the agent's speech to 0.85x for learners and capped calls at two minutes, with a daily limit on the server so the credits can't all go in one day. Hanging up uses the built-in end_call tool. Its description tells the model to use it only after your question is dealt with and you've said you don't need anything else, not when you just say thanks. Explain question opens a second, text-only session with a helper prompt, so the explanation never ends up in the call transcript. Slow replay uses ElevenLabs text to speech (Flash v2.5 at 0.7x).

The agent has had 113 conversations so far. ElevenLabs groups them by topic on its own, and the top three match the examples in the app: booking an appointment (27), the washing machine (19) and a missed delivery (17).

ElevenLabs agent dashboard: 113 conversations, with topics grouped as Appointment Booking and Scheduling (27), Washing Machine Issue Resolution (19) and Missed Delivery Redelivery Request (17)

Why I switched to a custom LLM
When I started, the agent used one of the LLMs hosted by ElevenLabs, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. Its usage came out of the same ElevenLabs credits I got for Hacktoberfest, and it was going through them fast. ElevenLabs lists it at about $0.016 a minute and $0.003 a message, on top of the voice. A custom LLM costs nothing on the ElevenLabs side:

The ElevenLabs LLM picker: hosted models with their prices, including Qwen3.5-397B-A17B at about $0.0159 per minute and $0.0030 per message, and Custom LLM at $0.0000

I wanted those credits for the voice, so I switched the agent to a custom LLM and pointed it at Gemma 4 31B on DigitalOcean, which bills my DigitalOcean account instead. With the per-token prices my tracing code uses for Gemma ($0.18 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens), the turn in the trace further down cost about $0.0002. The ElevenLabs credits now only pay for the audio.

At first the custom LLM pointed straight at DigitalOcean. Later I put my own server in between so I could trace and check every reply. This is the agent's LLM setting now:

The agent's Custom LLM setting in ElevenLabs: Chat Completions, server URL https://before-i-call.onrender.com/llm/v1/ and model ID gemma-4-31B-it

On each turn, the agent sends the conversation to my FastAPI server on Render, the server forwards it to Gemma 4 31B on DigitalOcean's serverless inference, and the response streams straight back, so the voice can start as soon as the first words arrive.

Architecture: the browser talks to ElevenLabs over WebRTC; ElevenLabs calls the Gemma proxy on Render, which streams Gemma 4 31B from DigitalOcean and sends traces to Sentry

The proxy on Render
The custom LLM URL points at my own server: a FastAPI app that Render runs as one Docker web service. The same service serves the React app, the API and the proxy. The whole setup is a render.yaml Blueprint in the repo (trimmed here):

services:
  - type: web
    name: before-i-call
    runtime: docker
    plan: starter
    healthCheckPath: /api/health
    disk:
      name: usage-data
      mountPath: /var/data
      sizeGB: 1
    envVars:
      - key: LLM_PROXY_KEY
        sync: false
      - key: GRADIENT_MODEL
        value: gemma-4-31B-it
      - key: MAX_CONCURRENT_CALLS
        value: '2'
      - key: MAX_CALL_SECONDS
        value: '120'
      - key: MAX_CALLS_PER_VISITOR_DAY
        value: '3'
Keys are sync: false, so they're set in the Render dashboard and never committed. The limits that protect my credits are plain environment variables: two calls at once, two minutes each, three calls per visitor a day. The 1 GB disk holds the SQLite files for those limits and the analytics, so they survive redeploys.

The proxy is a single route. It accepts only the agent's key, refuses every model except Gemma 4 31B, and passes DigitalOcean's stream through unchanged while it reads each chunk for tracing and the rule checks (trimmed):

@router.post('/llm/v1/chat/completions')
async def chat_completions(request: Request):
    ...
    if not isinstance(body, dict) or body.get('model') != model:
        # The key is never usable for other, more expensive models.
        raise HTTPException(400, f'Only {model} is available.')
    ...
    async def relay():
        async for chunk in response.aiter_bytes():
            stream.feed(chunk)
            yield chunk

    return StreamingResponse(relay(), media_type='text/event-stream',
                             headers={'Cache-Control': 'no-cache', 'X-Accel-Buffering': 'no'})
An always-on web service suits this. Each reply is a streamed response that stays open while Gemma talks. The server reuses one HTTPS client for DigitalOcean, so a turn doesn't pay for a new TLS handshake. And when you interrupt the AI, ElevenLabs drops the request, so the proxy closes the stream and records the turn as cancelled in Sentry.

Here's the proxy at work in Render's logs, one line per Gemma request from the agent:

Render application logs filtered to POST /llm/v1/chat/completions: a steady list of 200 OK responses on October 4 and 5

The service is managed by the Blueprint, which stays synced to the repo, and every push to main deploys on its own:

Render Blueprints page: before-i-call, synced with adkbbx/before_I_call on main

Render events for the before-i-call web service (Docker, Starter, Blueprint managed, live): deploys started by 

Fixing how numbers are read
The first version read 7時 as "nana-ji". Nobody says that. Japanese numbers change their reading depending on the counter after them: 7時 is しちじ, 10分 is じゅっぷん, 4月1日 is しがつついたち and 2人 is ふたり. Dates, times and the number of people are exactly what you say on a phone call, so this had to be right.

I fixed it with a pronunciation dictionary: 118 entries I wrote by hand plus 5,989 generated ones for dates, clock times, durations and counters, 6,107 in total. A script builds the rules and uploads them to the ElevenLabs agent as a pronunciation dictionary, and the app uses the same list for slow replay and the recorded demos. The text on screen doesn't change. This is the dictionary on the agent:

ElevenLabs agent settings: the pronunciation dictionary 

Japanese voices trip over dates and counters, so I wrote 6,107 fixes: 7時 is shichiji, not nana-ji

Tuning the prompt for Gemma
Switching to Gemma meant rewriting the prompt. I tested it with text-only runs of the agent. The old prompt never called end_call (0 of 2 scenarios), and the tuned one hung up in all 4. It also keeps ordinary words in kanji and writes numbers in kana so the voice reads them correctly, and it asks for practice details instead of your real ones. It still missed the hang-up sometimes in real calls, and Sentry caught that. The start of the tuned prompt:

The start of the agent's system prompt in ElevenLabs: polite spoken Japanese, one question per turn, kanji for ordinary words, numbers with counters in hiragana such as 7時→しちじ, and never inventing dates, prices or availability

Checking every reply with Sentry
Since every turn goes through my server, I can check each reply against the rules of the practice call. If you said goodbye and the AI didn't hang up, if it "confirmed" a booking, or if it put digits or English letters into Japanese speech, that becomes a Sentry issue tagged with the prompt version and turn number. Each request is also a gen_ai trace with time to first token, token counts and estimated cost. After a call you can tap Report this reply, and the report shows up next to that turn's trace. Conversation text only goes to Sentry if you choose to attach it.

Here's a real one. On October 3, the practice partner didn't hang up after the learner said goodbye, and Sentry caught it 8 times in four minutes. Each rule gets its own issue:

Sentry issue feed showing one unresolved issue, Practice partner: missed hang up, on /llm/v1/chat/completions with 8 events

The issue lists every time it happened and which release it came from:

The missed hang up issue in Sentry: 8 events between 5:57 and 6:01 PM UTC on October 3, all on the same release in production

For comparison, here's a turn where the partner did hang up. The execute_tool end_call span is the hang-up. The Gemma call took 1.27 s (Sentry's average for it is 1.49 s), used about 1,100 input tokens and 43 output tokens, and cost less than a cent. Traces don't include the conversation text, so the Input tab is empty.

A Sentry trace of one practice turn: invoke_agent, chat gemma-4-31B-it taking 1.27 s, the end_call tool and the request to DigitalOcean, with 1.1K input tokens, 43 output tokens and a cost under $0.01

All of those Gemma calls run on DigitalOcean's serverless inference, so I never had to run a GPU server. In two days, October 3 and 4, the app sent about 1.28 million input tokens to Gemma 4 31B and got about 75,000 back. Most of it is input because every turn sends the instructions and the conversation so far, while the replies are short, like the 43 tokens in the trace above.

DigitalOcean Serverless Inference, Analyze tab: 1,278,483 input tokens and 74,719 output tokens, all used on October 3 and 4

Bugs I hit along the way
Gemma sometimes wrote voice directions like [calm] or [pause] into its replies. The app strips them from the text on screen.
Small models sometimes say a tool call out loud, like end_call(reason="done"), instead of calling the tool. The app removes that text before it's spoken and treats it as a hang-up.
Running Gemma 4 locally, the first replies came back empty because the model spent all its tokens on hidden reasoning. Setting reasoning_effort: "none" fixed it, and replies now take about half a second on my laptop's GPU.
Kokoro's Japanese voice wouldn't install on Windows, because pyopenjtalk needs CMake to build. pyopenjtalk-plus has prebuilt wheels, so I switched to that.
Romaji showed 10月4日 as "10tsuki4hi". Romaji and furigana now use the same reading list as the voice, so it reads juugatsu yokka.
Why Does Open Innovation Matter?
The hosted version runs on paid APIs. I also wanted a version that's free and private, so the same code can run entirely on a laptop. With LOCAL_VOICE=1, Whisper handles speech recognition, Gemma 4 E2B (4.3 GB, through Ollama) plays the other person, and Kokoro-82M speaks. Explanations, slow replay, Enhance prompt, the word list, furigana and the PDF all still work. Nothing is sent to a provider, it works offline, and you can switch models with one setting (LOCAL_LLM_MODEL).

Same app, two brains: Gemma 4 31B on DigitalOcean with ElevenLabs, or Gemma 4 E2B on a laptop with Whisper and Kokoro

On my laptop (Ryzen 9 5900HS, RTX 3060 with 6 GB), the AI greets you in 2.4 s, answers what you say in about 6 s, and an explanation takes 1.4 s.

A free local practice call: Gemma's reply with furigana and romaji, a tap-to-speak microphone and the call controls

The local version isn't as good. The ElevenLabs voice sounds more natural, responds faster and lets you interrupt it. Locally you tap to talk, and the small model doesn't follow the role-play rules as closely as the 31B. It's possible at all because Gemma's weights are open: the same model family runs on DigitalOcean and on my laptop, with the same prompt, rules and pronunciation list. Furigana and romaji don't need a model. The open-source pykakasi and Janome libraries handle them.

Prize Categories
Best Use of ElevenLabs: one agent over WebRTC for every call, with per-call prompt, first line, language and voice overrides, the built-in end_call tool, a custom LLM pointed at Gemma, a separate text-only session for explanations, text to speech for slow replay, and a 6,107-entry pronunciation dictionary on the agent.
Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing: every Gemma request is a gen_ai trace with time to first token, tokens and cost. Replies are checked against the role-play rules, and user reports link to the exact turn.
Best Use of DigitalOcean: serverless inference runs Gemma 4 31B for every call turn, explanation, prompt enhancement and word list, with no GPU to manage.
Best Use of Gemma: Gemma does four jobs (the other person on the call, the explanation helper, the prompt enhancer and the word picker), as 31B in the cloud and E2B on a laptop.
Best Use of Render: one Docker web service from a render.yaml Blueprint serves the app, the API and the custom LLM proxy that streams every Gemma reply to ElevenLabs, with a persistent disk for usage limits and analytics, keys kept out of the repo, and the credit limits as environment variables.
Built solo.

If you live in Japan and put off phone calls too, try it and tell me in the comments what's missing.

    d = D(470)

    rows = [("Qwen3.5-4B, untuned", 18, 10, 28, False), ("Gemma 3 4B", 23, 13, 35, False), ("Gemma 3 12B", 45, 33, 57, False), ("Mochi fine-tune (v2)", 88, 78, 95, True)]
    for i, (n, v, lo, hi, acc) in enumerate(rows):

        d.o.append(f'<line x1="{x0 + lo * sc}" y1="{y + 20}" x2="{x0 + hi * sc}" y2="{y + 20}" stroke="{INK}" stroke-width="2.4"/>')

    d = D(h)

## How I Built It
### The big picture
A request makes two lanes run **at the same time**: one for visuals and one for language. They meet at the deck and the video, which need the finished copy.
![System architecture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/system.png)
The page polls the job every 1.5 seconds and shows real progress and partial copy as it arrives. Nothing is faked.
### Which model does which job
Every model has **one job and one strict contract**.
![Models and their jobs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/models.png)
| Model or tool | Job |
|---|---|
| **Gemma 3 4B** (Ollama) | Fast copy (the default), reading photos |
| **Gemma 3 12B** (Ollama) | Best-quality copy, and the independent judge in my evaluation |
| **rembg** (U2-Net) | Cuts the product out of its background |
| **OpenCV, NumPy, Pillow** | Measure, denoise, 2x upscale, fix tone, build the deck. Deterministic. |
| **FFmpeg** | The video. Camera moves, crossfades, text cards. **Not** generative video. |
| **Qwen3.5-4B + LoRA** (Tinker) | My fine-tuned copy writer |
| **A plain-code checker** | Scores and flags the copy |
Two choices worth explaining.
**The video is not AI-generated.** It's image processing plus FFmpeg. That means the product in the video is *your* product, pixel for pixel. Generative video tends to repaint the product, and a seller can't se
**The checker is plain code, not a second model.** A model can talk itself into anything. A word list and a number check can't.
### The copy pipeline
![Copy pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/copy.png)
The kit is split into small parts that run in parallel: four core parts plus one per platform. Each part's output is forced into a JSON schema. A bad call is retried once, and only the missing parts are redone.
### Reading your photos
![Photo reading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/photo-reading.png)
Up to 5 photos go in. Each one is shrunk to 768 px and read under strict rules. What comes back is only ever a **suggestion**, marked "From photo, check it". It never goes straight into your copy.
### Photos to studio shots
![Studio imagery pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/studio.png)
Measure the photo, cut out the product, clean the product's pixels, fix the tone, choose a backdrop that suits what the photo shows, then compose. If the cutout looks wrong (too little or too much of the frame)
### The video
![Video pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/video.png)
The plan has at least 4 shots. Each is rendered with FFmpeg, up to 3 at once, then joined with 0.4 s crossfades. Text cards come from your edited copy. The result is checked to be 10 seconds (plus or minus 0.5)
### Why it's fast
My first version was far too slow. One big generation on a laptop took 90 to 145 seconds.
![Before and after: what the Fast default and parallel parts bought](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/speed.png)
Three changes fixed most of it:
| Change | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Fast mode (Gemma 4B) as the default | copy 53 s | copy 14 s |
| Split the kit into parallel parts | one 12B call, 90 to 145 s | 45 to 60 s |
| Run the visual and language lanes together | the sum of both | the slower lane, plus a few seconds |
A four-photo kit went from about **100 s to about 18 s** in Fast mode. Best quality (Gemma 12B) takes about 57 s.
The trade-off is real. The 4B model gets more claims flagged than the 12B. The post-check still catches them, and Best quality is one switch away.
### Training a small model to follow the rules
This is the part I'm proudest of.
![Fine-tuning pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/finetune.png)
The idea: a big teacher model writes marketing kits, code and an independent judge reject any kit that breaks the rules, and only the **clean** kits are used to train a small student.
### Did it work?
Tested on 60 held-out synthetic products the training code refuses to read.
![Evaluation results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/evaluation.png)
The full table and what it does and doesn't prove are in the Tinker section below.
### What Sentry sees
Every model call is traced, and nothing a seller typed ever leaves the machine.
![What Sentry sees, and what it never sees](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/observability.png)
### Privacy by design
*Where your data can and can't go.*
![What stays local and what can leave](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/trust.png)
Your product facts stay on your computer. The only things that can ever leave are a Shopify draft you tap, and scrubbed Sentry metadata. Both are covered in the sections below.
## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?
Go back to my two stories. In both, the real cost was not money alone. It was **control**.
**1. Your product details are your business.**
Pricing, ingredients, launch plans, the way you describe your product. With open models running locally, all of it stays on your machine. There is no "we don't train on your data" to trust. The data never leaves.
**2. A fixed price of zero, per kit.**
On your own computer, every kit costs electricity. A seller can run it five times on one product, try three tones, and never wonder if it is "worth" the credits. In a business where cashflow is tight, that matters.
**3. I could change the model, not just the prompt.**
The most important thing I did in this project was fine-tune a small open model so it follows one rule better: *don't invent claims*. Prompting alone left the 4B model at 23% clean kits. Training took it to 88%. You can't do that to a closed model, and you can
**4. I could look inside and measure.**
I tested the fine-tune against a second, independent model as a judge, not just my own checker. With a closed API I'd have had one number and no way to question it.
**5. One setting swaps the model.**
Fast or Best quality is a single setting, and both are open Gemma models. The next Gemma release is a one-line change.
The honest limit: open models on your own computer need a computer that can run them. I wrote the local setup into the README.
## My Agent Session
I built Mochi with Claude Code, and every session is recorded with **Entire**. Each commit carries the checkpoint of the conversation that produced it.
- [`docs/DECISIONS.md`](https://github.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/blob/main/docs/DECISIONS.md) lists **19 decisions**, each with its reason, its commit and its Entire checkpoint ID
- About **113 checkpoints** are pushed to the repo
- To read one: `entire checkpoint explain <id>` in a clone of the repo
Two of the decisions the record shows, in my own words:
- **#10: a regulated-claims check for cosmetics.** A skincare seller can't say "reduces wrinkles". It's a legal claim, not a style choice.
- **#16: making Fast the default.** Stage timings showed copy was the slowest part, so the default became the smaller model.
One caveat on honesty: checkpoints for work from before Entire was switched on were *imported* from my local history and matched to commits by time. Read those as "the conversation this came out of", not a one-to-one record. The decisions file says the same.
## My First User
**Velora**, a skincare brand, ran its **Sensicontrol Face Cleanser** through Mochi on a phone, on **16 October 2026**. I have the screen recording. Here is what happened, taken only from what is on screen.
I don't have a written quote from them, so I'm not putting words in their mouth. What I do have is the recording, and it shows what they actually did.
They followed the five steps above (the screenshots for steps 1 to 4 are from their session): three photos of the bottle, the label read off it, a persuasive tone, Best quality writing, Pinterest as the platform, and the warm and cozy backdrop.
**What came out** is shown at the top of this post: the finished kit in 55 seconds, the studio photos, the deck, the video and the copy. It was built on Best quality, with three photos, by a Gemma 3 12B model running on my own computer.
**The part I care about most.** Mochi told them what it *wouldn't* make up:
- **"Not provided, so left out of the copy":** dimensions, verified benefits, target audience, care instructions
- **"Double-check before posting":** *Not in your facts: "available now". Remove it unless it's true.*
- **"About your photos":** it skipped the close-up slide because the photo didn't have enough pixels on the product
![Mochi lists what it left out and what to double-check](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/velora/velora-06-double-check.png)
The kit was five slides, nine studio photos, a 10-second video, and copy for one platform.
**What I learned from watching.** All of this is from the recording:
- **They changed their mind before generating.** They started with the Friendly tone, Instagram and Fast, then switched to Persuasive, Pinterest and Best quality. The choices clearly matter to people, so I'm glad nothing is locked in.
- **They left several facts blank, and the copy respected that.** Target audience, dimensions, verified benefits and care instructions were never filled in, so Mochi left them out and said so, instead of guessing.
- **Best quality costs time.** The form says Fast takes about 20 seconds and Best quality about a minute. They chose the slower one, and it took 55.
## Prize Categories
I'm entering **Tinker, Gemma, Sentry Agent Tracing and Entire**. Each section covers what I used, why, what it was meant to fix, and what I found.
### Best Use of Tinker
**What I used it for.** I fine-tuned **Qwen3.5-4B with a LoRA adapter** on Tinker to write marketing copy that follows one rule: *never invent a claim the seller didn't give.*
**Why Tinker.** Prompting a small model to follow that rule didn't work. Untuned Qwen3.5-4B produced a clean kit only 18% of the time. I wanted to change the model, not keep rewording the prompt, and Tinker let me train without running my own GPU servers.
**How it worked.**
1. A big teacher model, **Qwen3.5-397B-A17B**, writes and revises kits on Tinker
2. My checker and an independent judge reject any kit with an invented claim, number or forbidden word
3. The teacher revises with the checker's findings, at most 2 rounds
4. Only kits with **zero** hard violations become training data
5. A small student is trained on those: rank 32, 3 epochs, 319 examples, learning rate 2e-4
6. A held-out set of 60 products, which the training code refuses to read, tests it
The whole thing cost **$5.41 of the $10 credit**.
The training pipeline:
![Fine-tuning pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/finetune.png)
**Results** (60 held-out synthetic products, one checker):
The evaluation:
![Evaluation results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/evaluation.png)
| Model | Clean kits | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.5-4B, untuned | 18% | 10 to 28% |
| Gemma 3 4B | 23% | 13 to 35% |
| Gemma 3 12B | 45% | 33 to 57% |
| **Fine-tune v2** | **88%** | **78 to 95%** |
That's a 4B model, a third of Gemma 12B's size, producing nearly twice as many clean kits, and about 10 times faster (4.9 s against 48.7 s per kit, though v2 runs on Tinker's cloud and Gemma on my laptop).
**Keeping it honest.** v2 trains only on kits that passed **both** my checker and an independent judge from a different model family (Gemma 12B), which lists every statement the facts don't support.
**The honest result on the judge.** v2 halves the untuned model's flags (0.43 to 0.20), but the confidence intervals overlap, and Gemma 12B is lower still at 0.13. With 30 kits per model I can't claim more than that.
**Limits I'm stating on purpose:**
- The test set is synthetic, and the checker also filtered the training data
- The fine-tune runs on Tinker, so its inputs leave the machine. The app's default (Gemma via Ollama) stays local.
- The fine-tune is **not** in the app's path yet. I haven't exported it to GGUF for Ollama.
- Hosted cost is about $3 per 1,000 kits, estimated from token counts
**What I learned.** A small model trained on the right examples can follow a narrow rule better than a larger model that's only prompted. The checker and the judge decide which examples count, so they matter as much as the training run.
### Best Use of Gemma
**What I used it for.** Gemma does three jobs inside Mochi, all through Ollama on the seller's own computer:
1. **The copy writer.** Gemma 3 4B for Fast, Gemma 3 12B for Best quality
2. **The photo reader.** It reads up to 5 photos and returns suggested facts, each tagged "From photo, check it"
3. **The independent judge.** Gemma 3 12B, a different family from the Qwen teacher, reviews kits in my evaluation
Which model does which job:
![Models and their jobs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/models.png)
How Gemma reads photos. It only ever suggests; you confirm:
![Photo reading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/photo-reading.png)
**Why Gemma.** It's open-weight, it runs on one machine, and it can be held to a JSON schema. That matters here: the seller's facts shouldn't leave their computer, and every part of a kit must come back as strict, checkable JSON.
**What it was meant to fix.** The cost and privacy problems from my ecommerce days: no per-kit fee, and nothing sent to anyone else's server.
**Results.**
- Both sizes run the same prompt and the same checker, so I could compare them fairly: **23% clean kits on 4B and 45% on 12B**
- Speed is the trade-off. Fast (4B) builds a four-photo kit in about **18 s**, Best quality (12B) in about **57 s**
- As the judge, Gemma 12B had the fewest flags of any model I tested (0.13 per kit)
What the Fast default bought:
![Before and after: what the Fast default and parallel parts bought](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/speed.png)
**What I learned.** Two things. First, the model size is a user choice, not a technical one, so I made it a switch on the form. Second, the judge is Gemma, so it may be lenient toward Gemma's own writing. That bias favours the Gemma rows and works *against* my
### Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing
**What I used it for.** Tracing every model call and every job, without Sentry ever seeing a seller's product facts.
**Why this was the hard part.** A marketing tool handles a seller's most private material: product details, prices, plans. Sending prompts to a tracing service would break the promise the whole product makes. So the question was not "can I trace this", it was 
**What Sentry sees.**
What Sentry sees and what it never sees:
![What Sentry sees, and what it never sees](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/observability.png)
- Each model call is a **`gen_ai.chat` span**, with the model, token counts and latency
- Each generation job is a transaction
- Each flagged claim is an issue (which rule fired, and how many)
- Each seller report is an event. The report button sends a section name and a fixed reason code, **never free text**
The flagged claims come from the copy pipeline's post-check, so each issue is a rule the code caught, not a model's opinion:
![Copy pipeline and its post-check](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/copy.png)
**What it never sees.** An allow-list scrubber removes everything that is not on the list of allowed metadata. Product facts, copy, photos and prompts can't pass it.
The trust boundary:
![What stays local and what can leave](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/main/docs/images/post/trust.png)
**How I know it works.** A canary test pushes a unique fake product through every input path of the real app, then fails if that marker shows up in *any* outgoing Sentry payload. It's in `tests/test_tracing.py`.
**Results and honesty.** The scrubber and the canary test are in place and pass. I am **not** claiming Sentry has caught a real production incident, because it hasn't. Mochi has had one real user session, not production traffic.
**What I learned.** Making tracing safe was a bigger design question than turning it on. The allow-list approach (what's permitted, not what's blocked) is the one that survives new fields being added later.
### Best Use of Entire
**What I used it for.** To record how Mochi was built, so a reader can see *why* the code is the way it is, not just what it does.
**Why.** Most repos show a result. For a project where I changed my mind several times, the changes are the story. A privacy rule, a new default and a safety check each have a reason that a commit message can't hold.
**What came of it.**
- **About 113 checkpoints** of Claude Code sessions, pushed to the repo
- [`docs/DECISIONS.md`](https://github.com/advikdivekar/sellcraft/blob/main/docs/DECISIONS.md): **19 numbered decisions**, each with the reason, the commit and the Entire checkpoint ID
- Anyone can run `entire checkpoint explain <id>` in a clone and read the prompts, files and reasoning behind a decision
**The most useful example.** Decision #11 records why Sentry only ever gets metadata, and how the scrubber enforces it. That kind of reasoning normally disappears. Here it is written down, with the conversation that led to it.
**Honest limit.** Checkpoints from before Entire was enabled were imported from local history and matched by time. They show the conversation a commit came out of, not a one-to-one record.

55 seconds for the whole pipeline feels suspiciously fast, video gen alone usually burns through that. Does the clock include the video ads or is that copy and images only? Asking because I glue my own outreach tools together and the handoffs are exactly where my time goes 

what do i answer them?

Their guess is right on one point, and it's the one that matters, so answer it directly. Here's a reply you can paste:

> Fair question, I'd be suspicious too. **The 55 seconds includes the video.** The clock runs from tapping Generate until the kit is ready, and that covers the copy, the studio photos, the image deck and the 10-second video, with the text cards added at the end.
>
> The reason it's that fast is that **the video isn't generated**. It's image processing plus FFmpeg: I cut the product out of its photo, put it on a backdrop, and add camera moves, crossfades and text cards built from the copy. There's no diffusion or video model in the loop, so it doesn't have the cost generative video has. The trade-off is that it's a motion ad made from your own product photos, not new footage.
>
> The other part is that the visual and language work run **at the same time** in two lanes, so the wait is the slower lane plus a few seconds. That's the handoff problem you described. It's one job instead of several tools passing files around.
>
> A few caveats, to be straight about it. That run was 3 photos on the Best quality setting (Gemma 3 12B) on my own machine. Fast mode takes about 18 s for a 4-photo kit. These are single runs on my hardware, not an averaged benchmark. The timings and the steps behind them are in the repo (`docs/RESULTS.md`), and the recording shows the whole run.

**The 55 seconds is a true claim, but a few lines around it overstate things, and I'd fix those on the post.** The corrected wording is in `docs/WRITEUP.md` locally, and I haven't pushed it.

**What is accurate (no fix needed):**
- **The clock includes the video:** the "ready in 55 s" message appears only when the whole job finishes. That covers the copy, studio photos, deck and video.
- **"On a laptop":** your machine is a MacBook Pro with an M3 Pro chip, so it's a laptop.
- **"No video model":** the video is cut-outs, backdrops, camera moves and FFmpeg text cards.
- **The 55 s timing:** it matches the recording.

**What overstated, and the fix:**

| Where | What the post said | Problem | Now says |
|---|---|---|---|
| What I Built | "**Mochi does not make things up.**" | Your own Velora run contradicts it. The copy contained "available now" and Mochi flagged it. The evaluation also showed 12% of the fine-tune's kits had violations, and many more with the default model. | "Mochi **checks its own copy** for things you never told it. Models do invent claims, so plain code checks every kit." |
| My First User | "told them what it *wouldn't* make up" | One of the three items it showed was something it *had* written. | "…what it had left out, and what it had written that they never said" |
| How I Built It | "your product, **pixel for pixel**" | The pipeline denoises, upscales and retouches the product, so the pixels do change. | "not a regenerated lookalike. (I do denoise, upscale and retouch it.)" |
| What I Built | "product itself never repainted" | Same issue. | "the product is never regenerated" |
| My First User | "ran… on a phone" | The phone reached your computer over a Cloudflare tunnel. The post also says nothing leaves your machine. | Added: "the photos passed through Cloudflare for this demo. In normal use everything stays on the machine." |

None of these changes the core story, and the flag you showed is actually the better proof: the app caught its own invented phrase.
